analysis.one_liner: Requires politically active tax-exempt groups to disclose their biggest donors to the IRS again.
analysis.headline: Sen. Tester introduced the bill with 19 cosponsors, but the Senate Finance Committee never gave it a markup or vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have undone a May 2020 Treasury rule that lets social welfare groups, labor unions, and business trade associations leave their large donors' names off the tax returns they file with the IRS. It would have restored the requirement to report anyone giving more than $5,000 a year, and taken away the IRS's power to grant new waivers. The point was to give tax and law-enforcement authorities a way to see whether tax-exempt groups were being used to hide political money.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, tax enforcers, and law enforcement. The IRS would again see who is bankrolling 501(c)(4), (c)(5), and (c)(6) organizations, making it easier to catch tax-exempt groups being used to disguise political spending or foreign contributions. Donor names would go to the IRS, not be published, so the public benefit is indirect — through enforcement and audits — rather than through a public list.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the requirement that social welfare organizations (501(c)(4)), labor organizations (501(c)(5)), and business leagues (501(c)(6)) report the names and addresses of anyone contributing more than $5,000 a year on their annual IRS information returns.
Nullifies the final Treasury regulations published May 28, 2020, which had allowed those organizations to omit donor names from their returns.

Removes the IRS's authority to grant new exceptions to the disclosure requirement going forward, so the rule could not be quietly waived again by the executive branch (existing pre-July 2018 waivers stay in place).

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy donors to politically active nonprofits and the groups themselves. Donors giving over $5,000 to 501(c)(4), (c)(5), or (c)(6) groups would lose the anonymity they have had with the IRS since 2018, and the organizations would bear the administrative cost of collecting and reporting donor information. Critics also warned that routing donor data through the IRS creates a record that could be used for political targeting of donors.

drawbacks.text: Donor information goes to the IRS, not to the public — annual returns under section 6033 do not publicly list donors — so the transparency gain reaches voters only indirectly, through audits and enforcement rather than through disclosure anyone can read.

The bill imposes a real compliance burden on thousands of groups, including labor unions and community nonprofits, and conservative organizations argued after earlier disclosure episodes that IRS-held donor lists invite politically motivated scrutiny of donors.

It overrides a regulation that was itself issued to implement a 2018 change in law and policy, so groups that had reorganized their finances around donor anonymity would have had to reverse course mid-stride for returns filed after enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest and indirect: it does not create a public donor database, it simply gives the IRS and law enforcement back the visibility into big-dollar political giving that existed before 2018. The costs are a compliance burden on nonprofits and unions and a privacy trade-off that routes more personal financial data through the IRS. For voters who want to know who funds political influence campaigns, the trade favors disclosure; for small charities, it is mostly paperwork.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Finance Committee, where the bill was sent on the day it was introduced, never scheduled a markup or a vote, so it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Tester introduced the Spotlight Act on February 3, 2021, joined by 18 other sponsors — 18 Democrats and the independent Sen. Angus King.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote appear in the record for the rest of the 117th Congress.
The Treasury regulations the bill targeted — allowing 501(c)(4), (c)(5), and (c)(6) organizations to omit substantial-donor names from their IRS returns — remained in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Big donors to politically active tax-exempt groups and the groups themselves are better off: they keep the donor anonymity with the IRS that the May 2020 rules allowed, and no one was ever forced to defend or vote against the disclosure requirement on the record.

for.name: Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 18 additional Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 18 of 48 Senate Democrats plus 1 of 2 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, including Sens. Wyden, Whitehouse, Warren, Brown, and Klobuchar.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.role: Chair, Senate Finance Committee (also a cosponsor)
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but, as chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled it for a markup or vote during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Business trade associations and conservative advocacy nonprofits
against.role: Outside supporters of the 2020 donor-secrecy rules
against.what_they_did: Had publicly supported the May 2020 regulation letting tax-exempt groups omit donor names, the rule this bill would have repealed.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 sponsors were Democrats or the independent Sen. King, but no vote was ever held, so there is no record of how anyone else — Republican or Democratic — would have voted.

industries.industry: Politically active 501(c)(4) social welfare groups and their donors
industries.note: These are the groups most often used to shield 'dark money' political spending. The bill would have forced them and anyone giving them more than $5,000 a year to disclose to the IRS, ending the donor anonymity the 2020 rules created.

industries.industry: Business trade associations and chambers of commerce (501(c)(6) leagues)
industries.note: Business leagues would have had to report their large donors to the IRS again, exposing the corporate and wealthy funders behind industry lobbying vehicles.

Unions would also have had to disclose substantial donors to the IRS. Some unions have their own reasons for donor privacy, though the largest financial flows in politics run through the (c)(4) and (c)(6) groups, not unions.
